Metal Roofing in Houston

Thinking about a metal roof on a house, a shop or a barn? Call one free number and you are put through to an independent, locally owned roofing company that installs and repairs metal roofs across greater Houston.

Why more Houston homeowners are asking about metal

Metal roofing in Houston used to mean barns, sheds and rural shops. It now shows up on farmhouse-style homes in new subdivisions, on renovated bungalows and on houses rebuilt after storms. The appeal is easy to see: long panels with few laps, systems that carry published wind uplift ratings, and finishes that can reflect a lot of Gulf Coast sun.

It is still a big decision. The price, the way metal behaves in hail and the way some insurance policies treat it all differ from a shingle roof. This page sets out the choices, the questions to ask and the rules that apply, so you can talk to a roofer with your eyes open.

Houston Expert Roofers does no roofing work. The number is a no-cost referral line. Day or night, its automated assistant asks what you have in mind and transfers you to an independent, locally owned roofing company that installs and repairs metal roofs. That company quotes and does the work.

Metal roof examples: the main types you will be offered

Most quotes in greater Houston come down to two families of panel, plus a few specialty products. The difference that matters most is how the panel is fastened.

TypeHow it is fastenedWhere you see itTrade-offs
Standing seamConcealed clips under raised seams; no screws through the face of the panelModern and farmhouse-style homes, higher-end re-roofs, low-slope sectionsFewer exposed holes to maintain; usually costs more and is harder to repair one panel at a time
Exposed fastener (ribbed or corrugated)Screws with rubber washers driven through the panel face into the deck or purlinsBarns, shops, carports, patio covers, some homesLower cost; hundreds of washers that age in the sun and need checking
Metal shingles, shakes or tile profilesInterlocking pieces shaped to look like other roofingHomes where the neighborhood expects a shingle or tile lookMay fit deed restrictions more easily; more pieces and laps than long panels

Panel makers' own comparisons describe exposed-fastener panels as the lower-cost choice and note that their screws must be checked and sometimes tightened over the life of the roof, while standing seam clips stay hidden under the seams.

Gauge, metal and coating

Steel thickness is sold by gauge, and a lower number means thicker metal. Residential steel panels are commonly 22, 24, 26 or 29 gauge. Angi's guide to gauges describes 24 gauge as the usual pick where heavy hail is common, 26 gauge for milder conditions and 29 gauge for sheds and outbuildings where looks matter less. Steel panels also carry a metallic coating under the paint, most often galvanized (zinc) or Galvalume (an aluminum and zinc alloy), and the two hold up differently around salt. If you live near Galveston Bay or Clear Lake, ask the roofer what the panel maker's warranty says about distance from salt water before you choose a metal.

Heat, wind and noise in a Houston summer

Heat and cool finishes

Roof temperature depends mostly on reflectance and emittance. ENERGY STAR cites Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory: a clean white roof reflecting 80 percent of sunlight stays about 50 degrees Fahrenheit cooler on a summer afternoon than a gray roof reflecting 20 percent. Berkeley Lab also tested cool pigments on metal panels: a cool brown reflected about 27 percent of sunlight, against about 8 percent for a conventional brown.

Wind uplift ratings

Metal panels are rated by uplift testing. For a TDI product evaluation, formed metal panels must be tested to UL 1897, UL 580, ASTM E1592 or FM 4474, and the published evaluations list how much uplift the panel resists at each clip or fastener spacing. Closer spacing usually means a higher rating, so the spacing on your roof should match the rating you are relying on.

Rain noise

The loud metal roof most people remember is on a barn with no deck and no insulation. Manufacturers note that panels over a solid deck, underlayment and an insulated attic sound much like a shingle roof inside the house. Ask what deck and underlayment the roofer plans to use.

Hail, cosmetic damage and your insurance

Hail can dent a metal roof without letting water in. That gap between how a roof looks and how it works is what insurance policies argue over. The Texas Department of Insurance lists four points for homeowners considering metal: a premium discount is not offered by every insurer and varies when it is; metal can still be dented by hail, debris and branches; a discount may come with conditions such as an exclusion for cosmetic damage; and coverage terms can change at renewal.

The idea goes back a long way. A 1998 TDI bulletin approved an optional homeowners endorsement that excludes cosmetic hail damage on impact-resistant roof coverings that earn a premium credit, defines cosmetic damage as a change in appearance that does not let water through or stop the roof from doing its job, and makes the endorsement void unless the policyholder signs it. The Texas Windstorm Insurance Association's manual also includes a cosmetic damage exclusion endorsement for residential policies.

None of this means metal is a poor choice. It means you should read the policy before you buy the roof:

  • Does my insurer give a discount for this roof, and how much?
  • Would a cosmetic damage exclusion be added, and how does the policy define it?
  • Is the panel rated for impact resistance under UL 2218, and does that matter to you?
  • What could change at renewal?

The deductible is yours to pay. The Texas Department of Insurance says it is illegal for a contractor to offer to waive, rebate or absorb your deductible, and a contract of $1,000 or more paid with insurance money must include a notice saying so. A roofer also may not act as your public adjuster on a property it works on. Treat any offer to "cover the deductible" as a reason to call someone else.

HOAs, deed restrictions and permits

Many subdivisions around Houston have deed restrictions and an architectural review committee that approves roof materials and colors. Texas Property Code section 202.011 limits what a property owners' association can do, but its wording is about shingles: an association may not bar an owner who is allowed to install shingles from choosing shingles designed to resist wind and hail, to improve heating and cooling efficiency or to generate solar power, as long as they resemble the shingles allowed in the subdivision, are at least as durable and match the look of the surrounding property. A switch to standing seam panels is not clearly covered by that protection, so read your restrictions and get the committee's approval in writing before you sign a contract. Metal shingle and tile profiles exist partly for this reason.

Inside the City of Houston, a re-roof needs a residential roofing permit from the Houston Permitting Center; roof covering work up to 100 square feet in total is exempt. Suburban cities and the coastal windstorm area have their own rules, covered on each town page.

Coastal windstorm rules. In the Texas Department of Insurance's designated catastrophe area (Brazoria, Chambers, Galveston and the other first-tier coastal counties, plus, in Harris County, Morgan's Point and the parts of La Porte, Pasadena, Seabrook and Shoreacres inside city limits and east of State Highway 146), roof work must meet the windstorm building code and be inspected while it is under way. When it passes, TDI issues a certificate of compliance (form WPI-8), which the Texas Windstorm Insurance Association uses to decide whether it can insure the home. Ask the roofer, in writing, who schedules the inspection and when you will get the WPI-8.

Barns, shops and outbuildings on acreage

Out toward Magnolia, Tomball, Waller County and the rural edges of Fort Bend, plenty of properties have a shop, barn or carport under exposed-fastener panels. Those roofs need different care from a house: fasteners that have backed out or lost their washers, rust where panels overlap, trim lifted by wind and ridge caps that have worked loose. If a barn roof is leaking or rattling, mention it on the call and ask the roofing company you are connected with whether it works on outbuildings.

Tell the line whether it is a new metal roof, a repair or an outbuilding, and where you live. The local roofing company you are put through to sees the roof for itself and writes up its own price, which should name the panel, gauge and finish.

Questions to ask a metal roofing company

About the panel and the install

  • Standing seam or exposed fastener, and why for my house?
  • What gauge, what metallic coating and what paint finish?
  • Which uplift test or TDI product evaluation covers this panel, and at what clip or screw spacing will you install it?
  • Will you tear off the old roof, and what deck and underlayment go under the metal?
  • How will you flash walls, chimneys, valleys and pipe penetrations?

About paperwork and warranties

  • Can you send your certificate of liability insurance?
  • Will you pull the permit, and do I need HOA approval first?
  • What does the panel maker's paint and metal warranty cover near salt water?
  • What does your workmanship warranty cover, in writing?
  • What maintenance will this roof need, and how often?

How a metal roofing call works

  1. Call the numberAn automated assistant answers (832) 662-4107 at any hour and asks which service you need, since the line also takes heating, cooling, pressure washing and water damage calls.
  2. Describe the roofA leak, missing shingles, hail, a limb on the roof or an old roof you want looked at, plus your part of greater Houston and how urgent it is.
  3. Get put throughYour call is transferred to an independent, locally owned roofing company, which hears a short summary before it picks up.
  4. Deal with the roofer directlyIt inspects, quotes and does the work, and you pay it (or your insurer does, as you arrange). If it misses the call, it gets your name, number, city and need to call you back.

Texas has no state roofing license. No state agency licenses roofing contractors in Texas, and a 2025 bill to create one (HB 3344) did not reach a vote of the full House before the session ended. So check what you can: a certificate of liability insurance sent to you, a written contract with the full scope, a permit where your city requires one, local addresses you can drive past, and the shingle maker's warranty registration. Some cities also ask roofers to register. The line does not check any of this for you. How to check a roofer before you hire.

Questions Houston homeowners ask

Are metal roofs hotter than shingle roofs?

Not because they are metal. What decides roof temperature is mostly how much sunlight the surface reflects and how well it gives off heat. Bare metal reflects well but gives off heat poorly, which is why most residential panels are painted. ENERGY STAR cites Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory research that a clean white roof can stay about 50 degrees Fahrenheit cooler than a gray one on a summer afternoon, and lab-tested cool pigments let darker colors reflect more than ordinary paint. Ask the roofer for the panel color's rated reflectance. Attic insulation and ventilation matter just as much.

Will insurance cover a metal roof?

That depends on your policy, not on the roof. According to the Texas Department of Insurance, a premium discount for a metal roof may come with conditions such as an exclusion for cosmetic damage, meaning dents that change how the roof looks but not how it works may not be paid for, and that terms can change at renewal. Before you choose metal, ask your agent whether a discount applies, whether a cosmetic damage exclusion would be added, and how it defines cosmetic. The roof insurance claims guide covers claims in detail.

Are metal roofs good in Texas weather?

They can be, if the system matches the conditions. In greater Houston that means panels with a published wind uplift rating installed at the fastener or clip spacing the rating assumes, a light or reflective finish for the heat, a coating suited to salt air near the bay, and a clear understanding of how your insurer treats hail dents. A metal roof that is badly fastened or flashed will leak like any other. Ask the roofer to show you the uplift test or TDI product evaluation for the exact panel it proposes.

How much do metal roofing panels cost?

The line does not quote prices, and panel prices move with the steel market. What changes a metal roofing quote most is the panel type (standing seam usually costs more than exposed-fastener panels), the thickness of the metal, the finish, the size and complexity of the roof, whether old shingles are torn off, the underlayment, and the trim and flashing at every edge and wall. Ask for a written estimate that names the panel, gauge, finish and fastening method. The roof replacement cost guide explains how to compare bids.

How often do metal roofs need maintenance?

Less than many roofs, but not never. Exposed-fastener panels need the most attention, because the screws and their rubber washers sit on the surface and should be checked for loose, backed-out or worn fasteners. Standing seam panels hide their clips, so the checks focus on trim, flashing, sealant at penetrations and debris in valleys. A look by a roofer after any major hail or wind event is sensible. See the roof inspection page for what a visit should cover.
